idea-plugin.description:
Tasklane keeps a to-do list inside your project, one per repository, stored as plain XML next to the code. No account, no server, no network call: the tasks live in .idea/tasklane/ and are yours to commit or ignore.

It is built for the notes you take while you code — the ones that never survive the trip to an external tracker.

In the tool window

  • States are tabs, each with a live count. The count comes from the same pass that fills the list, so it never claims three over a list of two: the search and the view filter are already in it. Every tab keeps its own selection and its own folded groups, and the one you left open comes back when you reopen the project.
  • A card per task. A priority stripe down its left edge, the title over up to three lines, one line of the body, and badges for priority, due date, tags, links, images and date. Title and description render Markdown in place: bold, italics, code and strikethrough show their style, not their marks.
  • Expand a card with the chevron on its right to read the whole task without leaving the list — the full title, every line of the body, and the images it references, each one after the line that names it. Click an image to open it full size. The chevron only appears when the card is actually hiding something.
  • Select card text with the mouse and copy it with ⌘C / Ctrl+C. Escape clears the selection. Both keys stay out of the way while nothing is selected.
  • Open links with a single click, straight from the row. Plain URLs, www. addresses and Markdown links are all recognised, shortened for display and opened in full. Links inside code spans are examples, not destinations, and stay untouched.
  • Change the priority from the card: click its priority badge for the list of priorities with their colours, or use Priority ▸ in the context menu to change every selected task at once.
  • Move tasks between states with Move To ▸, or one tab at a time with ⇧⌥←/→ — no dialog either way. ⌥←/→ just switches the tab you are looking at.
  • Bookmark a task from its own row to pin it to the top of its group, whatever its priority: bookmarking is exactly saying "do not let me lose this".
  • Group by date, priority or tag — or not at all. Date sections run Today · Yesterday · This week · days · months · Undated against whichever date the state anchors on. Every header folds with a click or with ←/→, and both the grouping and what you folded are remembered per state.
  • Filter the view down to open, overdue or bookmarked tasks. It stacks with the search instead of replacing it, and clearing the search leaves it alone.
  • Search that understands operators and reads the whole body, not just the row, ignoring case and accents in both directions: state:, p:, repo:, is:, has:link|image|code, file: and #tag. Free text asks for every term; a half-typed operator is ignored rather than emptying the list.
  • One list per repository. Open several Git repositories in the same window and each keeps its own tasks, with a selector to switch — plus a toolbar toggle to search across all of them at once, which labels every row with the repository it came from.
  • Copy to the clipboard as Markdown or plain text: this whole tab, the date group the selection is in, or just the selected rows. With a search active you copy the search result, which is the only thing you can check before pasting. A date group comes out as the log of its day — ## 2026-09-11 and a numbered list — so it can be pasted into a journal or a weekly report as is.

In the task dialog

  • Write in Markdown, with a formatting toolbar for bold, italics, code, links, images and bulleted or numbered lists. It is the same dialog whether you create or edit, so a task jotted down in a hurry is not born different from one written calmly.
  • Images you can paste, drag or pick. A screenshot from the clipboard lands under the line your caret was on and shows up right there, scaled. ⌘Z undoes it like any other edit, clicking it opens it full size, and deleting its [image] marker removes it. Files are stored beside the tasks of their repository, named after the SHA-256 of their content: the same screenshot pasted into two tasks is one file, and what nothing references any more is collected when the project opens.
  • State and priority as dropdowns, seeded from the tab you were on.
  • A due date from presets — today, tomorrow, end of week, next week — or from a calendar. It falls due at the end of the day, so something set for today is not born overdue; once past, the card paints it red.
  • Tags as chips, typed separated by comma or space and removed with their cross. In the search field they are #api.
  • Code anchors as chips too, each one removable. They cannot be typed in by hand: an anchor is a place in the editor, and typing a path and a number is what this exists to avoid.
  • Priority triggers. Typing !!! Fix the login creates Fix the login at High: the prefix moves the priority dropdown as you type and is never saved. Longest match wins, a trailing space is required, deleting it gives the old priority back, and picking one by hand beats the prefix. Only when creating — an existing task should not lose its priority just because its body starts with !!!.
  • Escape closes the dialog even with the caret inside the body.

In the editor

  • Tasks that point at the code. New Tasklane Task from Here, in the editor's context menu, opens the dialog with the file, the line and the character already attached; anything selected comes in as the body. The card then shows an Auth.kt:42 badge that jumps back to that exact character, with the full path in its tooltip.
  • Anchors that survive edits. The line is stored with its text, not just its number, and is found again by that text when you follow it: an extra import, a re-indent or a moved function break nothing. If the line is gone the file still opens where it was, and if the file is gone you are told — a click that does nothing reads as a bug.
  • And the code points back. A line with an open task on it is marked in the colour of the task's priority. Hover the mark and the task is there — title, state, priority, due date, tags and its screenshots, so the one case where you must not have to open anything, an image, is the one it shows you. Click it and the tool window opens with that task selected, switching repository if the task belongs to another one.
  • Two marks, and you pick. A gutter icon, which never moves your code by a single pixel and lives where breakpoints already do; or an inline chip sitting on the exact character the task was about — because cache.get(key) ?: load(key) is two things in the same place. The chip carries the task's own state in capitals, like a code marker has for decades, so the factory setting reads TODO and a task in Doing reads DOING instead of lying. It keeps a little air on both sides so the code does not run into it, and that space belongs to the mark, not to your file. Or no mark at all, if you prefer.
  • Only what is still open gets marked. A task in a done state is history, not a note about the code, so its mark goes the moment you move it — and it goes then, not whenever an inspection next runs. Marks work the same in a .txt as in a .kt.
  • Several tasks in one spot share one mark, coloured by the highest priority among them, and the tooltip lists them.

From anywhere in the IDE

  • Quick Add with ⌘⌥R / Ctrl+Alt+R opens the full task dialog without going through the tool window. The task lands in the active repository.
  • Quick Add Task and New Tasklane Task from Here also sit in the Tools menu, and every Tasklane action is reachable from Search Everywhere.
  • Every action is in Settings → Keymap under Plugins → Tasklane, so anything you use daily can get a key of its own — including the ones that ship without one because they only mean something inside the tool window.

In Settings → Tools → Tasklane

  • States, as a table: name, which one is the default, which ones mean "done", how each groups its tasks, which date it groups by (created, updated or completed) and its colour in light and dark themes. The order here is the order of the tabs. Deleting a state asks where its tasks should go.
  • Priorities, the same way: name, default, colours, and the trigger you type to select it. The order here is the priority order.
  • Priority triggers can be turned off altogether.
  • Repository depth: how deep to look for repositories under the project root. It is a view filter, not a delete — a deeper repository that already has tasks is never hidden, and neither is one whose folder is gone.
  • Code anchors: gutter icon, inline chip, or no mark. This one is yours alone — it goes to workspace.xml and is not shared with the project.
  • Image size: the longest side pasted screenshots are scaled down to.
  • Save as template for new projects, so configuring per project does not mean configuring every project. And a direct link to the Keymap.

Where your tasks live

Tasks go to .idea/tasklane/, which the plugin auto-ignores, so nothing lands in your diff unless you ask for it. States and priorities go to .idea/tasklane.xml, which is meant to be committed: that is how a team shares the same workflow. Every write is atomic and keeps a backup, and a file it cannot read is quarantined instead of overwritten.

Requires IntelliJ IDEA 2025.2 or newer (any IntelliJ-based IDE). Git is optional: without it, the project root works as a single repository.
